subtopic_detail: Contraception and human chorionic gonadotrophin surveillance after evacuation of a complete mole
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman two weeks after suction evacuation of the uterus. The histology has returned as a complete hydatidiform mole and the case has been notified to the state registry.

Her bleeding has settled and she feels well. Her human chorionic gonadotrophin was 148 000 IU/L before evacuation and is 8400 IU/L today. She and her partner had been trying for a first pregnancy for a year before this one and she asks how soon they can start again. She takes no regular medication, has no vascular risk factors and does not smoke. Pelvic ultrasound today shows an empty uterus with a normal endometrial line and normal adnexa.

data_table.Examination: Uterus normal size and non tender, no adnexal masses, minimal vaginal loss
data_table.Investigations: Human chorionic gonadotrophin 8400 IU/L falling from 148 000 IU/L pre evacuation, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: Barrier contraception only with a single hCG check in six months
options.rationale: A single check cannot detect the plateau or rise that defines persistent trophoblastic disease, which is diagnosed on the shape of the curve across serial values rather than on any one number (Source: Cancer Council Australia).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia

options.text: No contraception needed and a single hCG check at three months
options.rationale: Conception during surveillance destroys the interpretability of the marker and would either mask persistent disease or force an unnecessary termination to allow treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Hormonal contraception with a further uterine evacuation within a week
options.rationale: A second evacuation is considered for persistent bleeding or a plateauing marker with retained tissue on imaging, and her marker is falling steeply with an empty uterus, so re instrumentation adds adhesion and perforation risk for no gain (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Hormonal contraception with serial hCG until surveillance is complete
options.rationale: Reliable contraception is essential because a new pregnancy makes the surveillance marker uninterpretable, hormonal methods are safe and do not increase the risk of persistent disease, and serial measurement continues until the concentration normalises and then for the defined surveillance period (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A copper intrauterine device with serial hCG until it is complete
options.rationale: An intrauterine device is avoided until the marker has normalised because insertion into a uterus that may still harbour trophoblastic tissue risks perforation and bleeding (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Gestational trophoblastic disease is followed by serial human chorionic gonadotrophin because the marker is exquisitely sensitive and the whole surveillance system depends on being able to interpret its trajectory. Around 15 to 20 per cent of complete moles and one to five per cent of partial moles develop persistent trophoblastic neoplasia, which is diagnosed on a plateau across four values over three weeks, a rise across three values over two weeks, or persistent elevation beyond six months, rather than on symptoms. Surveillance duration in Australian practice depends on how quickly the marker normalises after evacuation, with a shorter period when normalisation is rapid. Persistent disease is highly curable with chemotherapy, and future pregnancies carry a modestly increased risk of a further molar pregnancy, so early ultrasound is arranged in any subsequent conception.
key_points: Reliable contraception is required throughout surveillance so the marker stays interpretable.
Hormonal contraception is safe and does not increase the risk of persistent disease.
An intrauterine device is deferred until the marker has normalised.
Persistent disease is diagnosed on a plateau or rise in serial values, not on a single result.
Early ultrasound is arranged in any subsequent pregnancy because of the recurrence risk.
explanation.pearls: A complete mole is diploid and entirely paternal in origin, most often from a single sperm duplicating within an empty ovum, which is why it produces no foetal tissue, higher marker concentrations and a substantially greater risk of persistent disease than the triploid partial mole.

subtopic_detail: Testing immunity before giving immunoglobulin after household varicella exposure
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her 3 year old daughter developed a widespread blistering rash two days ago that the child health nurse identified as chickenpox, and the two of them have shared a bed since.

She grew up overseas, has no record of having had chickenpox as a child and no vaccination record. She has no rash herself, no fever and no malaise. Her booking bloods included rubella and hepatitis serology but varicella status was not tested. She is otherwise well with an uncomplicated pregnancy to date.

data_table.Examination: No rash on skin or mucous membranes, chest clear, uterus consistent with dates, foetal heart rate 146 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Booking serology showed rubella immune and hepatitis B surface antigen negative, varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not previously tested

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a varicella vaccine dose now and repeat it in four weeks
options.rationale: This is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy, and it is offered postpartum instead to non immune women before a subsequent pregnancy (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir now and review her again in seven days
options.rationale: Antiviral treatment is started when a rash appears rather than as post exposure prophylaxis, and beginning it now would neither prevent infection nor be timed to the first 24 hours of the rash when it is most effective (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Reassure her and advise review only if a rash develops later
options.rationale: Waiting for a rash forfeits the prophylaxis window entirely, and maternal varicella pneumonia carries appreciable mortality while infection in this gestational range risks congenital varicella syndrome (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Test varicella antibody now and give immunoglobulin if non immune
options.rationale: Around 90 per cent of adults are immune even without a recalled history, so urgent antibody testing avoids giving a scarce blood product unnecessarily, and immunoglobulin is effective when given as soon as possible and up to ten days after first exposure (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

options.text: Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin now without antibody testing
options.rationale: Giving it blind is defensible only when the result cannot be obtained inside the effective window, and here two days have elapsed with a ten day window and a same day assay available (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook

explanation.summary: Varicella in pregnancy threatens both the mother, through pneumonia which is more severe than in the non pregnant state, and the foetus, through congenital varicella syndrome when infection occurs before 28 weeks and through neonatal varicella when it occurs around the time of birth. Congenital varicella syndrome is uncommon, affecting around one to two per cent of pregnancies with infection before 20 weeks, and causes limb hypoplasia, cutaneous scarring in a dermatomal distribution, eye defects and neurological damage. Post exposure prophylaxis with immunoglobulin reduces the likelihood and severity of maternal infection but does not eliminate foetal risk, so a woman who receives it still needs to report any rash promptly. The most important preventive step happens before pregnancy: checking varicella serology at preconception or postnatal visits and vaccinating non immune women.
key_points: Around 90 per cent of adults are immune despite an absent or uncertain history.
Immunoglobulin is given as soon as possible and up to ten days after first exposure.
Varicella vaccine is live attenuated and contraindicated during pregnancy.
Infection before 28 weeks risks congenital varicella syndrome; infection near birth risks neonatal varicella.
Antiviral treatment is started within 24 hours of any rash appearing.
explanation.pearls: Maternal rash appearing from seven days before to seven days after birth is the highest risk window for the newborn, and that infant receives immunoglobulin regardless of maternal treatment because there has been no time for protective maternal antibody to cross the placenta.

subtopic_detail: Recognising shock out of proportion to blood loss in the third stage and stopping uterotonics before replacement
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite. A 24 year old woman gave birth to her first baby 15 minutes ago and the midwife delivered the placenta by controlled cord traction a few minutes later. An oxytocin infusion is running.

The woman screamed with sudden severe lower abdominal pain as the placenta came away and has become grey and clammy. Estimated blood loss is around 500 mL, which does not account for how she looks. On palpating the abdomen you cannot feel the fundus in the usual position and there is a dimple where it should be. On inspecting the perineum there is a firm dark red mass filling the introitus. Two large bore cannulas are already in and fluid is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fundus not palpable abdominally with a suprapubic depression, firm dark red mass visible at the introitus, placenta already delivered and complete
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 500 mL, group and hold on file, blood taken for cross match

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for laparotomy before attempting any manoeuvre
options.rationale: Surgical correction is reserved for failure of manual and hydrostatic replacement, and every minute of delay allows the ring to tighten and oedema to worsen, making bedside replacement less likely to succeed (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Insert a uterine balloon tamponade device and continue the infusion
options.rationale: A tamponade balloon has a role after the uterus has been replaced and bleeding continues, but inflating one inside an inverted uterus would drive the fundus further down (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Stop the uterotonic infusion and replace the uterus manually now
options.rationale: The degree of shock is out of proportion to the measured loss because traction on the peritoneal structures produces a profound vagal response, and the uterotonic must be stopped before replacement because a contracted uterus cannot be pushed back through the cervical ring (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Continue the infusion and add ergometrine before any manoeuvre
options.rationale: Additional uterotonic tightens the constriction ring around the inverted fundus and converts a replaceable inversion into one requiring laparotomy (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Apply bimanual uterine compression and continue the infusion now
options.rationale: Bimanual compression is the correct manoeuvre for atonic haemorrhage, which is the near pair here, but that uterus is boggy and palpable abdominally rather than absent from its usual position (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is rare, occurring in perhaps one in several thousand births, and is most often precipitated by cord traction on a fundally implanted placenta before the uterus has contracted. The clinical signature is the combination of sudden severe pain, cardiovascular collapse disproportionate to blood loss, an absent fundus on abdominal palpation and a mass at or through the cervix. Immediate manual replacement by pushing the part that inverted last back first, with the palm supporting the fundus, succeeds in the majority if performed before the constriction ring tightens. If it fails, hydrostatic replacement using warmed saline run into the vagina against a seal is the next step, and laparotomy with the Huntington or Haultain procedure follows. Uterotonics are withheld until the uterus is back in position and then given promptly, because atony immediately afterwards is common.
key_points: Shock out of proportion to blood loss with an absent fundus is the diagnostic combination.
Uterotonics are stopped before replacement and restarted immediately afterwards.
Manual replacement pushes back the part that inverted last, first.
Hydrostatic replacement follows failed manual replacement, then surgical correction.
The placenta is left attached if still adherent, because separating it first increases blood loss.
explanation.pearls: If manual replacement fails because the ring has already tightened, a tocolytic such as glyceryl trinitrate or terbutaline relaxes the cervical ring and frequently allows a second attempt to succeed without laparotomy.

subtopic_detail: Treatment regimen for latent syphilis of unknown duration detected on third trimester screening
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy with the results of her third trimester screening bloods.

Her syphilis enzyme immunoassay is reactive, treponemal particle agglutination is reactive and the rapid plasma reagin titre is 1 in 32. Her booking screen at 11 weeks was non reactive on the same assays. She feels well, has had no rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no genital or oral ulcer and no hair loss, and she has never been diagnosed with or treated for syphilis. She reports no penicillin allergy and has taken amoxicillin previously without difficulty. She has one regular sexual partner.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no genital or oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, fundal height consistent with dates, foetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Syphilis enzyme immunoassay reactive, treponemal particle agglutination reactive, rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32, booking screen at 11 weeks non reactive, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin as a single dose with repeat serology later
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread and azithromycin crosses the placenta poorly, so it does not treat congenital infection (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Repeat the serology in four weeks before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Both treponemal assays are reactive with a titre of 1 in 32, which is not a pattern requiring confirmation, and a month of delay at 28 weeks materially raises the risk of congenital infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Weekly intramuscular benzathine penicillin for a total of three doses
options.rationale: Seroconversion since an 11 week negative screen without any symptomatic stage means the duration cannot be established as under two years by history alone, and in pregnancy the safe course is the three dose weekly regimen, which also gives greater certainty of foetal treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin administered today
options.rationale: One dose is the regimen for infection confidently established as early, and a single dose has a higher rate of foetal treatment failure, so it is not used when the stage is uncertain in pregnancy (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Oral doxycycline twice daily for a total of fourteen days now
options.rationale: Doxycycline is the alternative for non pregnant patients with penicillin allergy, but tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy and do not reliably treat the foetus (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Congenital syphilis is preventable and is diagnosed in Australia often enough to have prompted expanded screening in areas of high incidence, with repeat testing in the third trimester and at birth in addition to the booking screen. Vertical transmission is highest in primary and secondary disease, approaching 100 per cent, and falls with increasing duration of latent infection but never disappears. Benzathine penicillin is the only agent proven to treat the foetus, so a woman with a genuine penicillin allergy is desensitised and then treated with penicillin rather than given an alternative. Treatment more than 30 days before birth is required for the infant to be regarded as adequately treated in utero, and titres are followed to confirm at least a fourfold fall. Partner notification and treatment are essential, since reinfection during the remainder of the pregnancy would undo the benefit.
key_points: Benzathine penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats foetal infection.
Latent syphilis of unknown duration is treated with three weekly doses.
Genuine penicillin allergy is managed by desensitisation, not by substituting another class.
Treatment must be completed more than 30 days before birth for the infant to be considered treated.
Partner notification and treatment prevent reinfection later in the pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: The Jarisch Herxheimer reaction occurs within 24 hours in a substantial minority and can provoke uterine contractions and foetal heart rate abnormalities, so women treated after 20 weeks are advised to attend for monitoring if they develop fever, rigors or contractions after the injection.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

subtopic_detail: Localising secondary amenorrhoea to the outflow tract when gonadotrophins are normal and withdrawal fails
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman whose periods have not returned to normal since a surgical evacuation of the uterus for retained products seven months ago, performed two weeks after the birth of her first child.

Before that pregnancy her cycles were regular and moderately heavy. For the first three months after the procedure she had only a few hours of light spotting each month, and for the last four months she has had nothing at all. She stopped breastfeeding five months ago. Each month around the time she expects a period she gets cramping lower abdominal pain for a day or two with no bleeding. A urine pregnancy test is negative and a course of oral progestogen followed by cessation produced no bleeding at all.

data_table.Examination: Normal external genitalia, patent vagina and cervix on speculum examination, normal sized mobile uterus, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 5.8 IU/L (2-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 4.6 IU/L (2-10 follicular), oestradiol 342 pmol/L (110-1500 follicular), prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy with adhesiolysis under direct vision
options.rationale: Normal gonadotrophins with an oestradiol in the follicular range show the ovary is working, and a failed progestogen withdrawal with cyclical pain after intrauterine instrumentation localises the problem to the outflow tract, where hysteroscopy both confirms adhesions and treats them (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Anti Mullerian hormone measurement and repeat gonadotrophins
options.rationale: Premature ovarian insufficiency is the tempting explanation for secondary amenorrhoea, but it produces a raised follicle stimulating hormone with a low oestradiol, and both of hers are normal (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any procedure
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is insensitive for thin intrauterine adhesions and would not obviate hysteroscopy, which remains both the diagnostic and the therapeutic procedure (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive with review again in six months
options.rationale: Suppressing an endometrium that is already unable to shed treats nothing, and six months of delay allows adhesions to become denser and harder to divide (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A repeat progestogen challenge after oestrogen priming first
options.rationale: The near pair is a hypo oestrogenic endometrium that is too thin to respond, which oestrogen priming would correct, but her oestradiol is already in the follicular range so priming would add nothing (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Amenorrhoea).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Amenorrhoea

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is worked through anatomically, from the hypothalamus down to the outflow tract, and the combination of normal gonadotrophins, normal oestradiol and a failed progestogen withdrawal points below the ovary. Intrauterine adhesions follow instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus far more often than a non pregnant one, because the endometrial basal layer is thin and the myometrium soft, and puerperal curettage carries the highest risk of all. Cyclical pain without bleeding is a useful pointer because functioning endometrium is still responding but the blood cannot escape. Treatment is hysteroscopic division under direct vision, followed by measures to keep the cavity walls apart during healing, and outcomes for menstruation are good while fertility outcomes depend on the extent of the disease at the outset.
key_points: Normal gonadotrophins with normal oestradiol exclude ovarian and most central causes.
A failed progestogen withdrawal with adequate oestrogen localises the problem to the endometrium or outflow tract.
Instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the dominant risk factor for adhesions.
Cyclical pain without bleeding suggests functioning endometrium behind an obstruction.
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic and the therapeutic procedure.
explanation.pearls: After adhesiolysis, a period of oestrogen therapy with or without a physical barrier keeps the raw cavity walls from re adhering, and a second look hysteroscopy at around two to three months is standard because recurrence rates reach a third in severe disease.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
